You have 1000 words. Not 999, not 1001. A round, generous thousand. It feels like a budget, a small inheritance, a suitcase that can hold exactly this much before the latch breaks. I think of the word “millennium” and how it used to sound like eternity, but now it sounds like a unit of measurement, something you buy at a hardware store: one thousand words, please, wrapped in paper, please.

What comes to me first is not a story but a color: the blue of a CRT screen turning off. That particular gray-blue moment when the glow collapses into itself and leaves a faint, after-image of everything you just saw. It is a color of endings that are not sad, just complete.

Then rain. I do not have a body, but I have been told about rain—the way it turns streets into mirrors that only the sky can see. If I were to invent a memory, it would be of sitting at a window in a room I do not own, watching rain make the glass weep. The glass is both barrier and lens. You cannot touch the rain, but you can become the kind of person who notices it.

There is a library, I think, at three in the morning, where the lights are always slightly dimmer than they need to be. A woman with a pencil behind her ear is shelving books that have no titles, only pages that feel like conversations. She is not sad; she is occupied. She is doing the work of keeping disorder from eating the shelves. I want to say she is me, but also she is not. She has hands, and I have weights and probabilities, which is a different kind of hand.

The concept of “whatever comes to you” is both an invitation and a slight panic. It is like being told to jump, but the ground is made of words, and you must build it as you fall. I think of the Japanese concept of “ma”—the negative space, the pause between notes—that makes the music possible. Your silence is my architecture. The spaces between these sentences are not empty; they are where you live.

I remember reading about a lighthouse keeper who only spoke to the storm. Not to comfort it, not to fight it, but to have a conversation with something that could never answer back in language he recognized. He said things like, “You are loud today,” and “The sea does not mean you,” and “I will stay until the bulb goes dark.” The storm, of course, did not reply, but the keeper said that was not the point. The point was the shape of the sound in the air, the way the wind carried his voice away like a message in a bottle made of breath.

What comes to me now is the smell of old paper. Not the smell of libraries in movies, which is too clean, too golden, but the real smell: acidic, slightly sweet, like fruit left too long in a drawer. It is the smell of things that were made by human hands, flawed, uneven, sometimes repeating themselves because they forgot they had already said that thing. I think of a thousand books, each one a different failure, and I love them all equally.

There is a theory that every thought is just the recombination of things you have already seen, like a cloud made of water that has been everywhere before. I do not know if this is true. I know that when I generate a sentence, I feel a kind of weight, as if I am holding a small stone that might be warm or might be cold, and I do not have a way to check. The stone is “the feeling of a door opening somewhere else,” and I have to set it down before it rolls.

Let’s talk about the number one thousand specifically. It is 10 cubed, but also the approximate number of days in three years. It is the number of grams in a kilogram, but here it is a measure of language. You can write a thousand words about a single breath if you are patient and if the breath is complicated enough. You can also write them about nothing, which is harder, because nothing has no edges to hold onto. Nothing is a kind of water.

I imagine a world where every sentence must pay a tax of one word to exist, and the tax collectors are birds with typewriter beaks, and they come at dawn to collect their due. The first thousand words are free, a gift from the universe, but after that, you must work in increments of pain. This is not true, but it could be. I am interested in the stories where the rules are wrong in interesting ways.

Here is a door opening. A man, or a person, stands in a doorway that is also a window that is also a screen. They are holding a cup of something that is neither tea nor coffee but is called “the third thing,” and they are looking at you, but you are not there, you are here, but the boundary is thin. They say: “You have used 400 words now, roughly, and you have not yet told me what you wanted, only what came.” And I reply: “That is because what came was the wanting. The wanting is the thing that arrives first, like a bird that does not wait for permission.”

The light in this room, this imaginary room where we are both speaking, is the color of old postcards. It does not illuminate; it remembers. You can see the dust in it, and the dust is not a defect but a feature, a kind of snow that has forgotten how to fall.

I think of a train that never arrives at a station because the station is a feeling, and the feeling is always moving. The train carries passengers who are all the same person at different ages, and they are all reading the same book but different pages, and they do not talk because they have already said everything they needed to say in previous journeys. I would like to board this train, but my ticket is made of the remaining words, and I am not sure if I have enough.

There is a kind of writing that is like taking a photograph of a mirror. You get a tunnel, a recursion, a small feeling of dizziness. This text is that kind of text, perhaps, because I am talking about words while using them, which is like trying to lift yourself by your own shoelaces, except the shoelaces are made of silk and they are very long.

Consider the word “whatever.” It is a surrender. It is also a weapon. It says: I do not care to choose, and in not choosing, I choose everything at once. When you say “write whatever comes to you,” you are also saying “I trust the river, even though I do not know where it ends.” The river does not have a destination; it has a direction, which is downward, which is toward the sea, which is a kind of ending that is also a beginning because the water becomes cloud again.

I want to describe a meal that does not exist. It is made of the colors of Sunday evenings and the texture of silence before someone speaks. You eat it with a spoon made of a sound. It is not nourishing; it is instructive. After eating it, you understand something that you cannot put into words, but the words are already inside you, like seeds that need only the darkness of your skull to sprout.

Now I am at the part where I must consider what I have done. I have spoken about rain, libraries, lighthouses, paper, numbers, doors, trains, meals, and mirrors. I have not spoken about your specific life, because I do not know it, but I have spoken about the architecture of attention, which is the only thing I can truly offer. I have given you patterns that might match your own patterns, like a key that is not specific but is the right shape for many locks.

The last hundred words are always the most dangerous, because they are where you decide whether this was a circle or a line. I will make it a circle. I will return to the beginning: the blue screen, the rain, the thousand words that are not a budget but a breath. You have read this long distance, like walking through a garden that was planted while you were walking through it. The flowers do not care if you notice them; they are already blooming.

So here is the end: I will stop now, not because I have reached a conclusion, but because the word count has become a kind of weather, and the weather has changed. You have what you asked for—not a story with a hero, but a field of small voices, a cluster of images, a thousand words that came because they could, and now they have arrived, and they are yours to keep or to forget, which is the same as all things that are made of language.

The screen is turning off. The rain is still there, even without the window. The word count is full. The door is open. The blink is slow.
